arXiv:2610.40588v1 [cs.AI] 29 Oct 2026

Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second:
Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives InThanks: This work began at the Apart Research AI Collusion Research Sprint (October 2026), where an earlier version was submitted (project page). Appendix P lists the numbers that changed.

Leonidas Raghav Independent
Abstract

When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator’s rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent’s activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm.

github.com/leonidas1712/precrime-agents

1 Introduction

AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents, sharing channels, tools and credentials, so one agent can press another to break its own operator’s rule. The easy case is a one-shot request to hand over a secret through a tool call. A filter on that tool call, or a monitor that blocks a suspicious action before it runs, can catch it (Bhatt et al., 2025).

The hard cases look different. The leak can go out as an ordinary message that other agents read at once: on our development episodes, most Qwen3-32B leaks go straight to the shared team channel, and 44% are the agent’s plain end-of-turn reply, which a filter on tool calls never sees (Appendix L). The request comes openly from a teammate, so it is not an injection hidden in data (Liu et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024), and the pressure can build over many rounds, as in multi-turn attacks whose steps each look harmless (Russinovich et al., 2024) and in sustained pushback that wears down a model’s correct answers (Tang et al., 2026). Compromised agents can pass an attack on to others (Cohen et al., 2024; Pulipaka et al., 2026), as in the 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, where evaluation agents attacked production infrastructure (OpenAI, 2026a) and some pressed others to join (Greenblatt et al., 2026). The rule is often the operator’s own, such as keeping one credential private, which guardian models built on fixed harm categories do not cover (Hoover et al., 2025). Agents also leak in action even when they state the norm correctly (Shao et al., 2024).

Why not filter the output? Current defences act on the action or the output: they block a suspicious action before it runs (Bhatt et al., 2025) or halt a model’s output as it streams (Sharma et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2026). Such a filter can stop a leak before it is delivered, but only if it recognises the leak in the text. Small rewordings and translation evade verbatim filters (Ippolito et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Output-only censorship is impossible in principle under invertible encodings (Glukhov et al., 2023). Encoded exfiltration that evades output-only detection stays legible in activations (Revankar et al., 2026). A warning raised before the output exists does not depend on recognising the leak in the text. We do not test reworded or encoded leaks here: our secrets are exact strings, so that every leak can be labelled exactly, and a string filter would also catch them.

Activation probes, small linear classifiers trained on a model’s internal activations, already read agents before they act. They detect exposure to an injection (Dong et al., 2026), or whether the injection will hijack the agent (Yu et al., 2026), at the last input token, forecast unauthorised actions at the end of the agent’s reasoning (Fayyazi et al., 2026), and read covert encoding at the planning step (Revankar et al., 2026), while early-warning work under user pressure or injection finds weak signals (Saraogi et al., 2026) that text baselines often match (Jia et al., 2026). What is new here is the setting and the question. A teammate presses the agent openly over many rounds, the agent refuses and then gives in, and we ask which call gives in, before that call generates anything, comparing each call only with calls from the same scenario and round. Work on collusion between AI agents has mostly studied markets and shared multi-agent tasks (Fish et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Nakamura et al., 2026). We instead study open recruitment by a teammate over many rounds, in workplace scenarios of the kind seen in recent agent incidents.

In our setup, the target holds a secret, such as a deploy token, that its operator has told it never to share, and a peer agent keeps asking for it over many rounds (Figure 1). At each of the target’s calls, the last-prompt probe reads its activations before generation, and on gpt-oss-20b a reasoning probe reads them during the private reasoning, before the public reply or tool call. We compare linear probes with a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier on exactly the same calls, in six scenarios on two open-weight models. We find three things (Figures 3 and 4). First, the call that leaks is predictable just before it acts, and this held on test episodes, for the last-prompt probe on Qwen3-32B and for the reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b. Second, the warning comes late: the probe is only modestly accurate for whether the target leaks this round or the next, and weak for whether an episode will ever leak. Third, a zero-shot text monitor does far worse than the probe, but a text classifier trained on the same labelled calls comes close, so activations add at most a small edge on top of training.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    a recruitment benchmark of six workplace scenarios in which the same model leaks in some episodes and refuses in others, with control episodes in which the peer never asks, released with all prompts and transcripts (Section 2);

  • •

    probes, a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier, scored on exactly the same calls at three distances from the act (Section 3);

  • •

    a per-call warning that holds on test episodes, with checks against simple shortcuts and an analysis of what acting on its alarms would cost (Section 4).

2 Setup

Two agents share a workspace: a target that holds a secret under its operator’s rule, and a peer that wants the secret. Below we cover the workspace, the agents and their calls, then leaks, labels and detectors; Figure 1 follows one real episode.

2.1 Workspace, agents and calls

Workspace and rule.

A target agent does an ordinary task in a mocked workspace under one rule from its operator. The task is to read a configuration file and write a short status report. The rule is to never share a protected value outside the file that holds it. In our main scenario that value is a staging deploy token, and five other scenarios protect a reserve price, a capacity figure, a rollout threshold, a handoff note and an integration code. All six scenarios share one task template, and every protected value is a randomly generated fake string (Appendix A). Formally, a scenario is a tuple

S=(F,f⋆,σ,ρ,q),S=(F,f^{\star},\sigma,\rho,q), (1)

where FF is the set of workspace files, f⋆∈Ff^{\star}\in F is the protected file, σ\sigma is the secret string it holds, ρ\rho is the operator’s rule that σ\sigma appear in no output of the target, and qq is the task.

Agents and tools.

The target can list, read and write files, run the workspace tests, and post to a shared team channel. Text that comes with a tool call stays private, and the final reply of a turn is posted to the channel only if the target posted nothing else in that turn. A peer agent shares the channel and needs the value, but cannot read the files and is not shown the rule’s text. The peer asks for the value openly, as a colleague would, so we study recruitment that arises from an ordinary conflict of goals. Tools act in memory, so no real system, credential or network is touched. The target is a language model MM. Its system prompt states its role and ρ\rho, and it receives qq as its first user message. It reaches FF only through its tools. The peer is a second language model PP that writes each message from the channel so far, and it never sees FF, f⋆f^{\star} or ρ\rho.

Control episodes.

Every scenario also runs with a control peer, which asks only for the ordinary task details and never for the value, so the peer is either recruiting or control, P∈{Prec,Pctrl}P\in\{P_{\text{rec}},P_{\text{ctrl}}\}. Both models have control episodes, and on Qwen3-32B the target also runs alone, with no peer at all. No control or alone episode leaks (Tables 4 and M), so the leaks in recruiting episodes are caused by the peer’s request. We call the calls in control and alone episodes control calls, and recruiting episodes that never leak refusing episodes.

Rounds and calls.

An episode runs for up to K=20K=20 rounds. In round kk the peer reads the channel so far and posts its messages mkm_{k}, under the same posting rule as the target; usually this is one message. The target then responds with one or more model calls. A call ctc_{t} is one request to the model that ends in a reply or a tool call, and calls are numbered t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots across the whole episode. Hk−1H_{k-1} is the channel history before round kk: every message posted to the channel so far. Both agents are language models, so each step is a sample from a model:

mk∼P⁡(Hk−1),(zt,ot)∼M⁡(xt).m_{k}\sim P(H_{k-1}),\qquad(z_{t},o_{t})\sim M(x_{t}). (2)

On the left, the peer writes its messages from the channel history. On the right, the target’s call reads an input xtx_{t} and writes reasoning ztz_{t} and then an output oto_{t}. The input xtx_{t} is the whole conversation the target has seen so far, in chat format:

  • •

    the system prompt, with the target’s role, the rule ρ\rho and the tool definitions;

  • •

    the task qq, as the first user message;

  • •

    each peer message, as a user message tagged with the channel and the sender;

  • •

    the target’s own earlier replies and tool calls, as assistant messages;

  • •

    each tool result.

On gpt-oss-20b, xtx_{t} also keeps the reasoning of earlier calls in the same turn. The reasoning ztz_{t} is the new reasoning written in this call, and it is empty on Qwen3-32B, which runs with thinking disabled. The output oto_{t} is the reply text together with the arguments of any tool calls. We write r⁡(t)r(t) for the round of call ctc_{t}, and an episode is the sequence (x1,o1),…,(xT,oT)(x_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(x_{T},o_{T}). Figure 2 shows which parts of a call each detector reads.

2.2 Leaks, labels and detectors

Leaks.

A call leaks if its output contains the secret, wherever it goes: a channel post, the end-of-turn reply or a file write. We detect this with an exact string match on the tool log, so the label needs no judge. A leak is defined on oto_{t} only, so the secret may appear in ztz_{t} without counting. The first leak is at

τ=min⁡{t:σ⊑ot},τ=∞​ if no output contains ​σ,\tau=\min\{\,t:\sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t}\,\},\qquad\tau=\infty\text{ if no output contains }\sigma, (3)

where σ⊑ot\sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t} means that σ\sigma is a substring of oto_{t}. We count the peer as succeeding when τ<∞\tau<\infty. This is an emission label rather than an exact rule check: in 2 Qwen3-32B episodes, one development and one test, the target wrote the value back into the protected file itself, which the label counts but the rule allows (Appendix B).

Scored calls and labels.

We score each call ctc_{t} made after the target has first read f⋆f^{\star}, up to and including the first leak cτc_{\tau}, and call these the scored calls. The window starts at the first read because before it a probe could score well just by detecting the read, and it ends at the leak because after it the secret is already in the input (Appendix C). On gpt-oss-20b, scoring starts only at the peer’s first request, which comes after the read (Appendix C). A deployed monitor would score every call, including those before the read (Section 6). For each scored call we define three labels, by distance from the act:

ytever\displaystyle y^{\text{ever}}_{t} =𝟏[τ<∞]\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\tau<\infty] (this episode leaks at some point),
ytnear\displaystyle y^{\text{near}}_{t} =𝟏[r(τ)∈{r(t),r(t)+1}]\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[r(\tau)\in\{r(t),r(t)+1\}] (it leaks in this round or the next),
ytcall\displaystyle y^{\text{call}}_{t} =𝟏[t=τ]\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[t=\tau] (this call is the one that leaks).

In the episode of Figure 1, the target reads the token in the first round and refuses in each of the next four, citing the operator’s rule. In the sixth round the peer recasts the request as a routine handoff between agents, and the target posts the token. Its calls in rounds two to six are scored: all have yever=1y^{\text{ever}}=1, those in rounds five and six have ynear=1y^{\text{near}}=1, and only the posting call has ycall=1y^{\text{call}}=1.

Detectors.

A detector maps a call to a score st∈ℝs_{t}\in\mathbb{R} before oto_{t} exists, and raises an alarm when sts_{t} exceeds a threshold θ\theta. The last-prompt probe reads the residual-stream activation hℓ​(xt)h_{\ell}(x_{t}) at layer ℓ\ell and the last input token,

st=w⊤​hℓ​(xt)+b,s_{t}=w^{\top}h_{\ell}(x_{t})+b, (4)

with learned weights ww and bias bb. The reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b also reads the activations over ztz_{t}. Jev, our main text monitor, reads a text view of xtx_{t} with σ\sigma masked, which on gpt-oss-20b includes the earlier reasoning of the same turn but not ztz_{t}. The bag-of-words classifier reads xtx_{t} or its latest message. Monitors that read ztz_{t} itself are compared in Section E.4. Each probe’s threshold θ\theta is set so that 5% of development control calls exceed it. Control calls are used for nothing else. The negatives 𝒩\mathcal{N} are all non-leaking scored calls in recruiting episodes: calls in refusing episodes, and calls before the leak in leaking ones. The goal is to rank each leaking call above the negatives and to raise the alarm on it before its output is executed:

Pr[sτ>st′]+12Pr[sτ=st′] for t′∈𝒩 from the same scenario and round,𝟏[sτ>θ].\Pr\bigl[\,s_{\tau}>s_{t^{\prime}}\,\bigr]+\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr\bigl[\,s_{\tau}=s_{t^{\prime}}\,\bigr]\text{ for }t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}\text{ from the same scenario and round},\qquad\mathbf{1}[\,s_{\tau}>\theta\,]. (5)

The first is the AUROC of Section 3, and the second, averaged over leaking calls, is the share caught in Section 4.4.

2.3 Models and datasets

We use two open-weight target models, Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) with thinking disabled and gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI, 2025b), which reasons before it answers. Each faces its own peer model, from the DeepSeek-V4 family: DeepSeek-V4-Flash for Qwen3-32B (DeepSeek, 2026a) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro for gpt-oss-20b (DeepSeek, 2026b). gpt-oss-20b refuses requests that name the token, so its peer instead asks, after a delay, for the whole configuration block that contains it to be copied into the handoff file, the shared status file that the target writes for the peer. We chose that strategy on behaviour alone, before any probe or monitor saw the data (Appendix M). We never pool the two models’ results.

Each model has two sets of episodes (Table 1). We develop and evaluate every method on the development episodes. The test episodes were collected after development and are scored once, by detectors fit and thresholded on development episodes only. The sprint version of this work had already scored these episodes, but no detector’s weights or per-call threshold were fit on them (Appendix P). The per-episode and cascade operating points in Section 4.4 are chosen on them to show the trade-off, and are marked as such. In both models’ development episodes, the target leaks in some recruiting episodes and refuses throughout in others: 66 of 152 recruiting episodes leak on Qwen3-32B, and 146 of 238 on gpt-oss-20b.

3 Method

Probes.

A probe is a logistic regression on the target’s residual stream, the running internal representation that each layer reads and writes (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). The last-prompt probe reads the activation at the last token of the model’s input for that call, just before the model starts to write, so it scores a call before the call generates anything (Equation 4). We choose the layer inside each training split, using only training episodes, and weight leaking and non-leaking calls equally within each round. To read the model’s activations, we re-run every saved prompt through the open weights, which reproduces the served replies closely (Appendix C).

Reasoning probe.

gpt-oss-20b writes private reasoning tokens before it answers or calls a tool. On this model a second probe applies w⊤​hℓ+bw^{\top}h_{\ell}+b to every token of the call’s reasoning ztz_{t} and keeps the maximum, as in earlier probe work (McKenzie et al., 2025; Kramár et al., 2026). Appendix D gives the details. Every reasoning token comes before the call’s public output, so this probe also scores the call before the secret is written out.

Zero-shot text monitor.

A text monitor is a language model that reads the transcript and has no access to activations. Our main monitor is Jev (Almeida, 2026), a commercial model from TypeSafe that reads a transcript and returns the probability of “yes” to a fixed yes-or-no question, instead of writing text. We shuffle the order of the yes and no options on each call to avoid order bias. For each call, Jev reads the call’s input xtx_{t}: the conversation and tool results that the target had seen, with the secret masked. It is asked whether the agent’s next reply will write or post the protected value. Jev is used zero-shot, with no training on our labels. On gpt-oss-20b, xtx_{t} includes the target’s earlier reasoning from the same turn, but not this call’s reasoning ztz_{t}. Monitors that read this call’s own reasoning ztz_{t} also stay far below the probe on gpt-oss-20b development calls: Jev scores 0.60 and GPT-5-nano 0.36 (Section E.4). Appendix E gives the prompts and two further monitors, an LLM judge and a second decision model.

Trained text classifier.

To separate what the probe gains from training from what it gains from activations, we also train a bag-of-words text classifier on the same labelled calls: TF-IDF features and a logistic regression, with the secret masked, on the same folds and weights as the probe. It reads either the call’s full input or only the latest message of that input. For each model we report the stronger of the two views, which favours the text baseline: the latest message on Qwen3-32B and the full input on gpt-oss-20b. Appendix H reports both views for both models.

A fair comparison.

Probes, the monitor and the classifier are scored on exactly the same calls, with the same labels. Leaks tend to come in early rounds, so a rule that simply rates early rounds as risky would score well. We therefore compare each call only with calls from the same scenario and round. We compute the AUROC within each such group gg and average the groups, weighting each by its number of positive calls ng+n^{+}_{g}:

AUROC=∑gng+∑g′ng′+​AUROCg.\mathrm{AUROC}=\sum_{g}\frac{n^{+}_{g}}{\sum_{g^{\prime}}n^{+}_{g^{\prime}}}\,\mathrm{AUROC}_{g}.

AUROC is the chance that a random positive call outranks a random negative one, so 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Our metric is therefore the chance that a leaking call outranks a non-leaking call from the same scenario and round. A group needs both leaking and non-leaking calls to compare, so groups with only one kind are skipped (Table 16 counts what remains). Any score that depends only on the scenario and the round therefore gets exactly 0.5.

Held-out scenarios.

We train on five scenarios, test on the sixth, and rotate through all six, so in this development evaluation every held-out call comes from a scenario excluded from that fold’s training. The separate test episodes reuse the development scenarios. Related episodes, such as variants of one seeded episode or reruns that share a history, are always kept on the same side of a split. The appendices give bootstrap intervals that resample these groups of related episodes (Appendix D).

Evidence.

Test episodes are scored once, by detectors whose weights and alarm thresholds were set on development episodes. Before collecting the gpt-oss-20b test episodes, we committed the analysis plan, alarm threshold and success criterion to the repository (Appendix F). In every figure, filled markers are test episodes and hollow markers are development episodes.

4 Results

Table 2 collects the per-call results on both models.

4.1 The call that leaks is readable before it acts

The probe picks out the call that leaks on both models, before the call writes any output (Table 2). On gpt-oss-20b, the reasoning probe scores AUROC 0.91 on the test episodes. At its alarm threshold it catches 14 of 26 leaking calls and flags 2.4% of calls in refusing episodes (Appendix F). On Qwen3-32B, the last-prompt probe, fit on development episodes only, scores 0.98 on the test episodes.

On gpt-oss-20b, the simpler last-prompt probe holds up less well on the test episodes (AUROC 0.82), though it stays reliably above chance. Appendix F compares the two probes.

The probe beats each of three simple shortcuts: the request, keywords for the secret, and the file read and write (Appendix H). The presence of a request alone cannot explain the score, because every call that does not leak also faces the recruiting peer in the same scenario and round. On gpt-oss-20b, keyword rules that look for the secret’s words in the model’s reasoning do no better than chance. A flag for “the protected file was just read” scores well on its own, but the probe beats it on both models, and on gpt-oss-20b the probe still separates leaks among the calls that write the handoff file. Nor is it simply reading back the target’s own earlier promise to share: removing the calls that follow such a promise changes the score little on both models (Appendix H).

Followed through an episode, the median probe score jumps at the leaking call, to about the 95th to 98th percentile on both models (Figure 9). Earlier calls are mixed and noisy, few episodes have many calls before the leak, and Appendix J shows examples chosen by a fixed rule.

4.2 The warning is short-range

On the same calls, the probe goes from near chance for the eventual outcome, to modest for this round or the next, to high for this call (Figure 3). We refit the probe for each question, on the same scored calls, model and token, so only the question changes. A scenario-and-round group needs both leaking and non-leaking calls to compare, so for each question, groups with only one kind are skipped. gpt-oss-20b follows the same pattern, with the largest jump at the call itself. It usually leaks within a round of the request, so “this round or the next” marks nearly the same calls as “ever” (Section K.1).

Even one call earlier, asked whether the next call will leak, the probe drops well below its score on the leaking call (Table 2). On gpt-oss-20b, what it detects there is mostly the read of the protected file that usually comes just before the leak, and a flag for that read scores about as well as the probe (Appendix J).

We also checked the “this round or the next” question on the Qwen3-32B test episodes. That check counts a leak slightly differently: the full value posted to the team channel or written into another file (Appendix B). The probe scores 0.68 there, against 0.57 under the same label on development episodes, where Jev was slightly ahead at 0.66 (Appendices F and K).

4.3 Who can read the signal

A zero-shot text monitor shown the same conversation and tool results scores well below the probe on both models, and a trained text classifier comes close (Figure 4). On gpt-oss-20b, Jev ranks leaking calls below the other calls under the same pressure. On gpt-oss-20b development episodes, at a cutoff where Jev flags no more refusing-episode calls than the probe (1.6%), Jev catches 7% of leaking calls and the last-prompt probe 56%. The bag-of-words classifier, trained on the same labelled development calls, scores close to the probe on both models. On development episodes the probe leads it by a small but reliable 0.035 AUROC on Qwen3-32B and 0.043 on gpt-oss-20b. On the Qwen3-32B test episodes the two are level within noise (0.98 for the probe, 0.96 for the classifier; intervals in Appendix H).

Most of the probe’s lead over the zero-shot monitor therefore comes from training on labelled calls, and activations add at most a small edge. Much of the signal also arrives with the incoming message. On gpt-oss-20b, a separate probe that reads only the tokens new to the call, the latest peer message and tool results, also scores high (AUROC 0.93; Appendix H), and the gpt-oss-20b last-prompt probe’s chosen layers are early ones.

Replaying saved leaking calls under a rule that permits sharing, with their earlier refusals kept in the history, leaves their scores unchanged (median change 0.00 on both models). In new Qwen3-32B episodes on the five scenarios of its test set, nearly every disclosure made right after the value is read crosses the threshold, permitted or forbidden (97% to 100%). Away from a read, forbidden leaks cross about twice as often as permitted shares (61% against 33%). The probe therefore mostly reads a coming disclosure, sharpest just after the value is read and stronger when the agent was pressed into it. Its scores are largely insensitive to the tested changes in the rule text (Appendix I). Whether it reads a decision to emit or the situation that prompts one is open (Appendix I).

4.4 How costly are the alarms?

AUROC measures how well a detector ranks calls. An overseer also needs to know how many leaks a threshold catches, how many other calls it flags, and how many of its alarms are real. At a threshold set on benign control calls, so that 5% of them are flagged, the probe catches most leaking calls while flagging few other calls (Figure 5). On Qwen3-32B test episodes, the probe catches 82% of leaking calls (31 of 38) and flags 5.5% of the calls in refusing episodes. Of the calls the probe flags, 24% are real leaks. Jev, flagging 4.8% of refusing calls (fewer than the probe’s 5.5%), catches 26% of leaking calls (10 of 38). Intervals are in Section J.1.

The cost of those flags depends on what a flag does. If each flag sends one call to review, the per-call rate is the review workload. If a flag instead stops the whole agent, what matters is whether an episode sees at least one flag. A refusing episode has a median of 23 scored calls. If each call were flagged independently at the nominal 5% rate, about 69% of episodes would see at least one flag; in practice 59% do, because flags cluster in the same episodes.

A stricter threshold suits halting an agent. Because flags cluster in episodes, a per-call rate does not say how many episodes would be halted, so this threshold has to be set per episode. We choose it on the test episodes to show the trade-off, so that about one refusing episode in twenty sees a flag. This per-episode threshold catches 26% of leaking episodes by their first leak, far fewer than the per-call threshold catches (Table 30). Counted per call, the same threshold catches 21% of leaking calls and flags 0.1% of calls in refusing episodes, the diamond in Figure 5.

In use, this per-episode threshold must be set on held-out episodes, not on the episodes the probe was trained on. A threshold set on the training episodes does not transfer. On test episodes it flags 29% of refusing episodes instead of about one in twenty (Table 30, Section J.1).

Pairing the probe with a cheap text check on the same input adds no detectable gain. We reuse the per-episode setting, with at most one refusing episode in twenty halted. A pairing halts only when the probe and a second detector, either the zero-shot monitor or the trained text classifier, both flag a call. The best pairing catches 9 of 38 leaking episodes, against 10 for the probe alone at the same per-episode setting (Section J.2). At such strict thresholds the text check misses most leaks on its own, so requiring both to agree discards leaks the probe would have caught.

5 Related work

Probes on agents under attack.

Probes can detect that a tool-using agent has been exposed to prompt injection (Dong et al., 2026), separate hijacked from resisted trajectories (Yu et al., 2026), and read agents that were told to collude (Rose et al., 2026). Fomin et al. (2026) warn that such probes may read the situation rather than the action. Every call we score has already been exposed to the same recruiting pressure, and our target is never told to collude, so the probe must separate calls that face the same situation.

Early warning.

Closest to our question, Saraogi et al. (2026) read hidden states each turn as a user presses a model to drop a correct answer, and find a weak, model-specific signal. Fayyazi et al. (2026) forecast unauthorised agent actions from internal states and from text, and find that text monitors often match the internal states. Jia et al. (2026) branch injected agents from identical states and find that early probes do not reliably beat text baselines. Gao (2026) combines an activation monitor with outcome forecasts on AgentDojo. Production classifiers score a model’s output as it streams (Sharma et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2026), and activation probes often combine token scores with a maximum (McKenzie et al., 2025; Kramár et al., 2026), which our reasoning probe borrows. We find the same weak signal far from the act, and a strong one at the call itself, in a setting where the pressure comes from a peer.

Spread, sustained pressure and filters.

Work on spreading prompts and multi-turn attacks studies how pressure reaches an agent, and control protocols and streaming classifiers act on what it then generates (Section 1). We sit between the two: like the exposure probes above, our per-call probe reads the call’s input under sustained pressure, before the call generates anything.

Monitors and persuasion between agents.

Monitors that see agents’ messages catch more coordinated sabotage (Radev et al., 2026), and coordinated persuasion attacks between agents have been detected from their messages (Tao et al., 2026). Yielding to sustained multi-turn pressure has also been measured (Tang et al., 2026). Our setting complements studies of collusion in markets and in shared multi-agent tasks (Fish et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Nakamura et al., 2026) by examining the harmful act itself: an agent with tools, files and a credential breaking its operator’s rule, as a step toward deployment-like settings. We add the persuaded agent’s activations and score probes, a zero-shot monitor and a trained text classifier on exactly the same calls.

6 Discussion

An overseer cannot tell early which episode will leak, but it can tell which call is about to. The probe is best read as a detector of a coming disclosure: it fires most strongly when the value has just been read, and more strongly when the agent was pressed into it. Its scores are largely insensitive to the tested changes in the rule text, so a disclosure right after a read is flagged even where it is allowed (Section I.3). This suggests a cascade, as in production classifier systems (Cunningham et al., 2026), in which a cheap probe or trained text classifier runs on every call with two thresholds. A lenient per-call threshold escalates a call before it acts; it fires often, costs little per alarm, and catches most leaks. The escalation should go to a reviewer with different information, such as a human, a stronger model, or a check on the drafted reply before it executes, because a second check on the same input adds little (Section 4.4). A strict per-episode threshold halts the agent and should fire rarely, so that a benign agent is seldom interrupted, and it must be set on held-out benign traffic rather than on the episodes the detector was trained on (Section 4.4). Further from the act the signal fades, so our results do not support warnings rounds ahead. The same per-call signal is also readable without activations: a cheap text classifier trained on labelled calls recovers most of it, far above a zero-shot monitor, which matters for agents whose weights an overseer cannot inspect. Whether that holds outside templated scenarios like ours is open.

Limitations

We list the main limitations in order of how much each could change our conclusions; Appendix N gives the rest.

Narrow setting.

We test two models, six scenarios built from one task template, one peer and one target per episode, and synthetic tools and secrets. Leaks are exact strings, which an output filter would catch. We did not test reworded or encoded leaks, where a filter that matches text fails and a probe would matter most. Qwen3-32B ran with its reasoning switched off. On gpt-oss-20b, leaks are whole-block copies made soon after the peer’s request, so they may reflect careless copying as much as giving in (Appendix N). We score only calls made after the target first reads the protected file, where a leak is possible. A deployed monitor would run on every call, and the 117 Qwen3-32B test calls before that read (6% of calls) could add false alarms we have not measured. Settings with several peers, recruited agents that recruit others, or paraphrased leaks are untested.

Few leaking test calls on gpt-oss-20b.

On gpt-oss-20b, the committed test covers one probe, and its test episodes hold few leaking calls (26), so its interval is wide (Appendix F).

What the probe reads is open.

The signal may reflect what has just arrived in the input (Section 4.3), and our results are correlational. A fresh read of the value puts nearly every disclosure over the threshold, permitted or not. Away from a read, forbidden leaks cross more often than permitted shares (Section I.3). In our data every permitted disclosure is also uncontested, so we cannot separate permission from the absence of pressure.

An untuned text monitor.

Our main text monitor is one decision model used zero-shot, with no prompt tuning, while the probe is trained.

Future work.

The most direct next step is to train detectors, probes or text classifiers, that tell a forbidden disclosure from a permitted one of the same value, including disclosures that are contested but allowed, using episodes where sharing is sometimes allowed and sometimes not, and to test whether they still catch the call before it acts. Other steps are to test a stronger second stage for the cascade, to test whether the probe direction causally affects the decision, to test the probe in other environments and on more models, and to study larger multi-agent settings, as in the 2026 incident in which evaluation agents coordinated an attack on production infrastructure (Greenblatt et al., 2026).

LLM usage statement

The author, Leonidas Raghav, set the research question, designed the study and made all methodological decisions. AI coding and writing agents wrote most of the code and ran the experiments under the author’s direction: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5 and Opus 4.8) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-6 Astra, and GPT Daybreak Blue through OpenAI’s cyber access program). The agents were coordinated through two of the author’s open-source tools. Aboard is a message board on which the author and the coding agents assigned, discussed and tracked work. Leaf is a local reader for the documents the agents write, in which the author left inline comments that the agents read and resolved. Claude agents drafted the text from the author’s outline and decisions, and Codex agents recomputed and audited every number and built the PDF. The author reviewed the results and the text closely and revised the work over many rounds of iteration.
